case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal district court that properly had original jurisdiction when it filed and then stayed a case pending arbitration retains jurisdiction to decide post-arbitration motions in that same case without having to identify a new, independent basis for subject-matter jurisdiction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially the provisions governing stays and post-award confirmation/vacatur motions, including FAA § 10); related background jurisdictional statutes implicated by the parties’ framing include federal-question jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1331) and supplemental jurisdiction (28 U.S.C. § 1367).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once a federal court properly has original jurisdiction over a civil action and enters a stay pending arbitration, the case remains a pending federal case and the court therefore retains continuing subject-matter jurisdiction to resolve the ordinary post-arbitration motions (e.g., confirm or vacate) without requiring the movant to plead a new, redundant jurisdictional hook; petitioner further contends that multiple circuits have already answered this question, that the Second Circuit’s approach is wrong as a matter of FAA structure and basic jurisdiction/continuing-case principles, and that any claimed “vehicle problems” (including petitioner having made alternative arguments) are not defects because alternative pleading is expressly allowed under the Federal Rules.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that Supreme Court review is premature because the circuit split is weak/underdeveloped and the case is a poor vehicle due to fact-specific circumstances; on the merits, respondents contend that a post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur request requires its own, independent jurisdictional basis (rather than relying on the pre-arbitration jurisdiction for the stayed action), and that the Second Circuit correctly treated jurisdiction for post-award relief as needing a distinct jurisdictional analysis rather than assuming continuing jurisdiction solely because the court earlier stayed the case pending arbitration.
key_precedents: Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen v. Erie R.R. Co., 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)
MasterCard Int’l Inc. v. Visa Int’l Serv. Ass’n, 471 F.3d 377 (2d Cir. 2006)
Beijing Shougang Mining Inv. Co. v. Mongolia, 11 F.4th 144 (2d Cir. 2021)
Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the hardest point: §§ 9–10 speak of an “application,” and Badgerow’s face-of-the-application rule cannot be evaded by procedural sequencing. But in the posture Justice Alito emphasizes (and Smith v. Spizzirri confirms), a mandatory § 3 stay leaves the same civil action pending; treating the post-award filing as a motion in that action does not “look through” a new application, it completes a case already properly within Article III and Title 28 jurisdiction. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction are not offended because the court is not manufacturing jurisdiction over a new controversy—it is exercising the ordinary power to resolve matters incident to a stayed case Congress told it to pause, and minimalism counsels against reading Badgerow to impose a silent dismissal/refiling trap when § 3 directs a stay. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern is mitigated by the objective, non-merits line here (stay versus dismissal), which allows a narrow holding that does not reopen Badgerow for freestanding § 9–10 proceedings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is their “continuing jurisdiction” framing: because a § 3 stay keeps the case on the docket (as Spizzirri confirms), the post-award request can be treated as merely a motion in the same action. But Badgerow’s rule is jurisdictional and attaches to the FAA §§ 9–10 “application” Congress created; § 3’s command to stay “the trial of the action” is procedural and does not purport to carry forward or supply Article III/Title 28 subject-matter jurisdiction for a distinct post-award application. Accepting the stay as a jurisdictional anchor would recreate look-through jurisdiction by sequencing—file a merits case with jurisdiction, stay, then obtain federal vacatur/confirmation without an independent § 1331/§ 1332 basis—an end run Badgerow’s text-based holding does not allow. Justice Kavanaugh’s Kokkonen analogy does not alter that, because ancillary jurisdiction cannot substitute for a missing statutory grant where Congress prescribed a separate “application” mechanism with its own timing and service rules.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that §§ 9–10 describe a distinct “application” with its own procedures, and Badgerow says jurisdiction must appear on the face of that application; I agree that § 3 does not itself “grant” jurisdiction. But that framing still does not answer the narrower question in this posture: when the court already has undisputed Title 28 jurisdiction over a pending civil action and merely stayed “the trial of the action” under § 3 (as Smith v. Spizzirri confirms keeps the case on the docket), the post-award filing is best treated as a motion in the same case—not a new, freestanding proceeding—so we are not doing forbidden look-through, just finishing the case we already properly have. Justice Thomas’s sequencing/end-run concern is real, but it would require us to impose a jurisdictional “reset” midstream based on the label “application” without a clear textual command in the FAA that a stayed case must be dismissed and refiled to obtain routine post-award relief. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction are satisfied here because the post-award relief is incident to resolving the stayed action to judgment, not an unrelated dispute, and I do not read Badgerow to silently displace that ordinary consequence of a § 3 stay.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s “continuing jurisdiction” account is the strongest point for Petitioner because it mirrors ordinary docket practice after a § 3 stay, and Justice Alito is right that Smith v. Spizzirri confirms the stayed action remains pending procedurally. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Badgerow ties jurisdiction to the face of the specific FAA §§ 9–11 “application,” and allowing a previously stayed merits suit to supply jurisdiction for a later confirmation/vacatur request functions as a sequencing-based workaround to Badgerow’s limit on look-through jurisdiction. Spizzirri answers only the procedural-status question (stay vs. dismissal); it does not identify any Title 28 grant authorizing federal adjudication of a post-award § 9/§ 10 application when § 1331/§ 1332 are absent at that stage, and Kokkonen cautions against using ancillary concepts to fill that gap. Given the jurisdictional nature of the rule and the availability of state-court enforcement, I would require an independent jurisdictional basis for post-award relief even when the earlier case was stayed.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito make the strongest case that a § 3 stay keeps the same civil action pending, so a post-award filing looks like a motion “within the case,” especially in light of Smith v. Spizzirri’s clarification of what a stay does procedurally. But that procedural continuity cannot do the jurisdictional work Congress did not do: Badgerow ties jurisdiction to the face of the FAA §§ 9–10 “application,” and § 3’s stay directive speaks to pausing “the trial of the action,” not to supplying or preserving federal subject-matter jurisdiction for a distinct, post-award request for relief. Justice Kavanaugh’s Kokkonen/ancillary-jurisdiction analogy does not persuade me because ancillary doctrine cannot substitute for a missing Title 28 jurisdictional hook where Congress has channeled post-award relief through a separate “application” mechanism with its own timing and service features. Pragmatically, adopting the stay-as-anchor theory would invite a look-through-by-sequencing workaround and make Badgerow’s administrable rule hinge on the happenstance of stay versus dismissal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito make the best case that a § 3 stay keeps the original civil action “pending,” so a post-award filing can be treated as a motion in the same case, with Smith v. Spizzirri reinforcing the procedural (not jurisdictional) point. But, as Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, §§ 9–10 create a distinct “application” mechanism with its own timing and service rules, and Badgerow ties jurisdiction to the face of that application—not to whatever once supported a stayed merits suit. Labeling the later request a “motion” cannot do the jurisdictional work Congress did not do; otherwise parties can evade Badgerow by sequencing (file a federal merits case, obtain a stay, then return for § 9/§ 10 relief without an independent Title 28 hook). Justice Kavanaugh’s Kokkonen-based ancillary-jurisdiction theory does not move me because Kokkonen warns ancillary jurisdiction cannot supply a missing jurisdictional grant for a distinct dispute Congress has separately structured.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the best textual objection: §§ 9–10 speak of an “application,” and Badgerow requires an independent Title 28 basis on the face of that application. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Alito’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri) that this posture is materially different: when the district court has entered a mandatory § 3 stay, the Article III case remains pending on the docket, and the post-award filing is best treated as a motion in the same jurisdictionally proper action, not a new freestanding proceeding that would trigger Badgerow’s face-of-the-application inquiry. Kokkonen’s limits on ancillary jurisdiction are a caution against manufacturing jurisdiction for unrelated disputes, but they do not require a jurisdictional “reset” midstream where the court is simply completing the stayed action in the narrow way the FAA contemplates. Justice Kagan’s sequencing/gamesmanship concern is real, yet the administrable line Roberts and Alito identify—stay versus dismissal—tracks § 3’s directive and avoids converting Badgerow into a trap for parties who followed the statute’s mandated procedure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “continuing jurisdiction” framing—bolstered by Justice Alito’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri that a § 3 stay keeps the action on the docket—does not answer Badgerow’s core point: FAA §§ 9–11 require an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of the post-award "application" seeking confirmation or vacatur. Treating a stayed merits suit as a jurisdictional anchor effectively recreates look-through jurisdiction by sequencing (file a federal merits action, stay, then obtain §§ 9–10 relief) despite Congress’s choice to structure post-award relief as a separate application with its own timing and service rules. Justice Kavanaugh’s ancillary/continuing-power theory runs into Kokkonen’s warning that ancillary jurisdiction cannot supply a missing statutory grant for distinct relief; docket management and “wrapping up” cannot substitute for Title 28 jurisdiction where Congress did not provide it. Smith v. Spizzirri clarifies the stay/dismissal distinction procedurally, but it does not create the jurisdictional hook that Badgerow requires for the later §§ 9–10 application.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is the textual/jurisdictional one: §§ 9–10 speak of an “application,” and Badgerow says jurisdiction must appear on the face of that application, so using the earlier merits suit as an anchor risks a sequencing-based end run. But in the § 3-stay posture that the Chief Justice and Justice Alito emphasize (and that Smith v. Spizzirri clarifies), the district court is not being asked to entertain a new, freestanding proceeding; it is completing the same still-pending civil action it already had Title 28 jurisdiction to hear, and the post-award motion functions as a procedural continuation needed to lift the stay and conclude the case. Kokkonen’s cautions about ancillary jurisdiction do not defeat that narrow continuation framing because the post-award relief is not an unrelated dispute—it is the congressionally contemplated next step in managing the court’s own docket after compelled arbitration. Pragmatically and procedurally, I do not read the FAA to impose a jurisdictional “reset” midstream that would penalize parties for complying with § 3’s mandatory stay and create an avoidable trap without clearer statutory command.

John Roberts.reasoning: Where a district court properly exercised original jurisdiction over a civil action and issued a mandatory stay under FAA § 3, the case remains pending on the court’s docket and the court retains jurisdiction to resolve post-arbitration motions in that same action without requiring a new, freestanding jurisdictional hook. Badgerow held that a standalone FAA §§ 9–10 application cannot use “look-through” jurisdiction, but it did not address (and should not be extended to unsettle) a court’s continuing jurisdiction over an already-proper federal case merely stayed for arbitration. This narrower disposition respects precedent and institutional legitimacy by harmonizing Badgerow and Vaden: Vaden governs “look-through” for § 4 petitions, while Badgerow limits new post-award proceedings—yet neither compels divesting jurisdiction in an existing stayed case. A contrary rule would create procedural traps and undermine the FAA’s structure, which contemplates stays (not dismissals) and efficient return to court for limited post-award review under § 10.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s text treats post-award relief as an “application” to the court under §§ 9–10, not as a continuation of merits adjudication, and nothing in § 3’s stay provision purports to expand Article III or statutory subject-matter jurisdiction. Under Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), a federal court may entertain a § 9 or § 10 application only when an independent jurisdictional basis appears on the face of that application; the court may not rely on the nature of the underlying dispute to supply jurisdiction. Allowing a stayed action to serve as a “jurisdictional anchor” would functionally evade Badgerow’s textual limitation and enlarge federal jurisdiction beyond what Congress has conferred in 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331 and 1332. Because federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, any continuing-jurisdiction theory must be grounded in statutory text, and the FAA provides none here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FAA § 3 directs that when an action is stayed for arbitration, the federal “proceeding” is stayed “until … arbitration has been had,” which presupposes the same case remains pending on the district court’s docket and may resume when arbitration concludes. That ordinary understanding of a stay, reinforced by Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472, 477–478 (2024), supports continuing jurisdiction to resolve post-award motions in the stayed action without demanding a new, duplicative jurisdictional hook, so long as the court properly had original jurisdiction at the outset. Requiring a fresh jurisdictional showing for post-award relief would create pointless traps and inefficiency inconsistent with the FAA’s pro-arbitration, streamlined framework while doing nothing to advance Article III limits where the underlying case remains live and anchored in an existing federal action. Badgerow’s “look-through” limits for standalone §§ 9–10 applications do not compel a contrary result when the post-award request is made within the same stayed case that already satisfied 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (or other original jurisdiction) at filing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), held that FAA §§ 9 and 10 applications require an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of the post-award application, and the FAA itself does not supply subject-matter jurisdiction. A stay under FAA § 3 pauses merits litigation but does not enlarge Article III jurisdiction; once the court’s work on the stayed claims is effectively complete, treating a later § 10 vacatur/§ 9 confirmation request as automatically within federal power risks creating an end-run around Badgerow’s limits. Requiring a fresh jurisdictional showing (e.g., 28 U.S.C. § 1331 or § 1332) for post-award relief is a clear, administrable rule that preserves the federal-state balance while leaving parties meaningful access to review in state courts. Although this may impose practical burdens on some litigants, the constitutional and statutory constraints on federal jurisdiction must control absent a clear congressional directive.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Badgerow v. Walters holds that FAA §§ 9–10 applications require an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of the application, and the FAA’s text does not create federal jurisdiction merely because the underlying dispute involved federal law. A § 3 stay keeps the pre-arbitration “case” on the docket, but it cannot expand Article III or statutory subject-matter jurisdiction to reach what is, in substance, a post-award § 10 (or § 9) proceeding that Congress treated as a distinct application. Nothing in the FAA links §§ 9–10 jurisdiction to the earlier existence of § 1331 jurisdiction in the stayed action, and treating stayed-case applications differently from “freestanding” ones would create an arbitrary, hard-to-administer jurisdictional rule contrary to Badgerow’s face-of-the-application approach. The better reading is that the district court may proceed post-award only if it can point to a valid jurisdictional grant (e.g., diversity, § 1331 on the application itself), not merely the historical fact that the case was once properly filed.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FAA does not itself confer subject-matter jurisdiction, and Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), instructs that post-award applications under FAA §§ 9–11 must rest on an independent jurisdictional basis rather than a “look-through” or other implied hook. Nothing in FAA § 3’s stay mechanism purports to extend Article III jurisdiction to later § 10 vacatur (or § 9 confirmation) applications if the court would otherwise lack statutory jurisdiction at that later stage; Congress knows how to create continuing-jurisdiction rules and did not do so here. The text of FAA §§ 9 and 12 contemplates an “application” served like a motion but does not override the baseline requirement that federal jurisdiction must exist for the specific proceeding, and § 1367 cannot be used to manufacture jurisdiction where the post-award application is not part of the same case-or-controversy over which the court retains statutory competence after arbitration. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles and this Court’s insistence that jurisdictional grants be clear, a district court must identify a valid jurisdictional basis for post-award relief even when the case was earlier stayed pending arbitration.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When a district court has original jurisdiction over a civil action and enters a stay under FAA § 3, the case remains pending on the court’s docket, and the court ordinarily retains power to resolve matters incident to that action—including the parties’ post-arbitration motions to confirm or vacate in the same stayed case—without demanding a new, independent jurisdictional hook. That conclusion fits traditional ancillary/continuing-jurisdiction principles recognized in Kokkonen, which allow federal courts to adjudicate matters incidental to a properly filed case, and it avoids the practical and workability problems of forcing duplicative filings or jurisdictional relitigation after arbitration. The Second Circuit’s requirement of a fresh jurisdictional basis for post-award relief, even when sought on the stayed docket, is difficult to reconcile with the FAA’s stay mechanism (§ 3) and with the Court’s emphasis on practical administration and coherent FAA procedure. Nothing in the FAA’s text clearly displaces ordinary continuing-jurisdiction principles here, and judicial restraint counsels against creating a jurisdictional trap that undermines the settled expectation that a stayed case returns to the same court for completion.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FAA’s text treats § 9–§ 11 confirmation/vacatur proceedings as “applications” that require their own jurisdictional footing, and Badgerow v. Walters held that such applications must establish an independent basis for federal subject-matter jurisdiction on the face of the application (rejecting “look-through” jurisdiction for §§ 9–11). Nothing in § 3’s stay mechanism purports to enlarge Article III jurisdiction or create continuing jurisdiction over a later § 10 motion, and reading a stayed case as an automatic jurisdictional “anchor” would effectively circumvent Badgerow’s limitation through procedural sequencing. The service and procedure provisions in §§ 9 and 12 further fit the understanding that Congress contemplated § 9–§ 10 applications as distinct proceedings, not merely post-stay motions that inherit jurisdiction without analysis. Consistent with methodological textualism and Badgerow’s emphasis on jurisdictional clarity, the district court must identify an independent jurisdictional basis for the post-award application even when arbitration followed a stayed federal action.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: When a district court properly has original jurisdiction and issues a stay under FAA § 3, the action remains pending; post-award motions to confirm or vacate are best understood as proceedings within the same Article III “case,” so requiring a new, independent jurisdictional hook is an unnecessary procedural trap that undermines efficient dispute resolution and predictable access to federal court. Badgerow v. Walters (2022) held that FAA §§ 9–11 do not themselves confer jurisdiction and rejected “look-through” jurisdiction for standalone post-award petitions, but it did not address—and should not be read to forbid—continuing or supplemental jurisdiction in an already-filed federal action that was merely stayed. At minimum, 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) authorizes jurisdiction over post-arbitration motions because they form part of the same case or controversy as the federal claims that supplied original jurisdiction, and nothing in the FAA creates a “positive repugnancy” displacing Title 28’s jurisdictional grants. A contrary rule, like the Second Circuit’s approach in Erie R.R. and its progeny, risks practical unfairness by forcing duplicative filings and forum whiplash after parties followed a federal court’s direction to arbitrate.

case_analysis.focal_point: When a federal court properly has original jurisdiction over a case and stays it pending arbitration under the FAA, does it retain jurisdiction in that same still-pending case to decide post-arbitration motions (confirm/vacate/modify) without needing a new, independent jurisdictional basis?
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1–16 (especially §§ 9–10 regarding confirmation/vacatur), and the federal courts’ subject-matter jurisdiction statutes implicated by the parties’ arguments (e.g., 28 U.S.C. § 1367 as referenced in the briefing).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that once a federal court has original jurisdiction at the outset and issues a stay pending arbitration, the court keeps jurisdiction over the same action and may adjudicate post-arbitration motions within that stayed case without requiring the movant to re-establish a separate jurisdictional hook. Petitioner emphasizes that multiple circuits have already resolved the issue, that the Second Circuit’s approach is wrong as a matter of jurisdictional doctrine and FAA structure, and that respondents’ claimed “vehicle problems” (including petitioner’s alternative arguments) are not genuine obstacles because alternative pleading is expressly permitted.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that the asserted circuit split is underdeveloped and that the Second Circuit’s unpublished disposition is a poor vehicle due to case-specific circumstances. On the merits, respondents maintain that after arbitration, a federal court should not proceed to decide confirmation/vacatur (or related post-arbitration relief) unless there is an independent basis for subject-matter jurisdiction for that post-arbitration request (i.e., the FAA does not itself supply jurisdiction and jurisdiction must be shown for the post-arbitration phase). They also argue petitioner’s predicted practical harms (forum-shopping/inefficiency) are overstated and speculative.

Smarter Tools Inc. v. Chongqing SENCI Imp. & Exp. Trade Co., 57 F.4th 372 (2d Cir. 2023)
Weiss v. Sallie Mae, Inc., 939 F.3d 105 (2d Cir. 2019)
Triestman v. Fed. Bureau of Prisons, 470 F.3d 471 (2d Cir. 2006)
MasterCard (Second Circuit precedent cited in the excerpt; full caption not provided in the supplied materials)
Union No. 2 United Ass’n of Journeymen, 841 F.2d 461 (2d Cir. 1988)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s central objection—that treating a §§ 9–11 motion in a stayed case as “ancillary” functionally recreates Badgerow’s forbidden look-through—is the strongest point for Respondent, but it still assumes the post-award request is a new freestanding “application” rather than a continuation of the same civil action Congress told us to stay under § 3. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes via Smith v. Spizzirri, § 3’s mandatory stay structure presupposes the parties’ return to the same federal case; unlike Kokkonen, there is no dismissal that terminates jurisdiction and triggers a need for a fresh jurisdictional hook. Our holding can be kept narrow and administrable: Badgerow continues to control standalone post-award filings, while in a properly commenced federal action that remains pending on a § 3 stay, the court may resolve post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur motions as part of completing that action without a jurisdictional “reset.” That approach respects precedent, avoids procedural fragmentation, and does not expand Title 28— it simply recognizes that a stay pauses proceedings without extinguishing jurisdiction already validly invoked.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that Badgerow requires an independent jurisdictional basis on the face of a §§ 9–11 “application,” and that treating a stayed case as “ancillary” risks recreating look-through jurisdiction by another name. But Badgerow addressed a freestanding, newly filed post-award proceeding; it did not hold that a federal court’s jurisdiction—properly invoked at the outset—evaporates midstream while the same “action” remains pending under § 3’s mandatory stay, a distinction Chief Justice Roberts correctly ties to Kokkonen’s dismissal/stay line. Textually, § 3 contemplates one civil “action” that is stayed “until” arbitration is had; when the parties seek confirmation or vacatur on the same docket, the court is completing that existing action, not entertaining a new suit, and nothing in the FAA or Title 28 imposes a jurisdictional “reset.” Justice Alito’s concern about bootstrapping would have force if the post-award filing initiated a new case, but here the court is exercising continuing authority over a stayed case already within Article III and an enumerated jurisdictional grant, so Badgerow’s no-look-through rule remains intact for standalone applications.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s ancillary-jurisdiction theory has intuitive appeal because a § 3 stay keeps the action pending, but docket continuity cannot supply the independent statutory jurisdiction that Badgerow demands for a §§ 9–11 “application” on its face; otherwise we recreate look-through jurisdiction by relabeling it “ancillary.” Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Smith v. Spizzirri strengthens the procedural point that stays (not dismissals) are required, yet Spizzirri did not purport to expand Title 28 jurisdiction, and “return to federal court” cannot be treated as a jurisdictional grant without turning § 3 into an end-run around Badgerow. Justice Thomas’s suggestion that ordinary ancillary/supplemental principles fill any gap is unpersuasive because using § 1367 (or ancillary power) to adjudicate a distinct post-award enforcement dispute would collapse Badgerow’s carefully drawn line whenever the front-end case happened to be filed in federal court. The practical consequence of Petitioners’ rule—federalizing state-law confirmation/vacatur disputes solely because a stayed federal case exists—confirms for me that the better textual reading is that §§ 9–11 still require their own jurisdictional footing.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito are right to worry that we cannot “recreate look-through jurisdiction by another name,” but their framing wrongly treats a post-award motion filed in a still-pending, jurisdictionally proper federal action as a freestanding new “application” that must independently satisfy Badgerow on its face. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh explain, a mandatory § 3 stay (reinforced by Spizzirri) preserves the court’s authority to finish the same case; unlike Kokkonen, there has been no dismissal that severs the court’s power and requires a separate jurisdictional hook. Badgerow can be respected by limiting its anti–look-through rule to standalone, newly initiated §§ 9–11 proceedings, while allowing courts to resolve confirmation/vacatur as ancillary steps necessary to conclude the stayed action—an approach that avoids forcing workers and consumers into fragmented, duplicative litigation. Under a pragmatic lens attentive to access to justice, the respondents’ rule would turn § 3’s stay into a procedural trapdoor with no clear textual command in the FAA or Title 28.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s best point is that Badgerow insists on an independent jurisdictional basis for a §§9–11 “application,” and that calling it “ancillary” could look like recreating look-through jurisdiction by another name. But that objection assumes the post-award filing is a new proceeding; as the Chief Justice notes, a §3 stay keeps the same civil action pending, and nothing in Badgerow says properly invoked jurisdiction dissolves midstream absent dismissal (Kokkonen’s scenario). Textually, §3’s “stay the trial of the action until” arbitration is had reads naturally to contemplate resumption—and Smith v. Spizzirri, as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, confirms the stay is designed so parties return to the same case, not restart jurisdictional showings from scratch. Limiting the rule to motions filed in the same stayed action preserves Badgerow for freestanding applications while avoiding the incoherent, fragmentation-inducing “jurisdictional reset” the FAA nowhere commands.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point is that Badgerow insists an independent jurisdictional basis must appear on the face of a §§ 9–11 “application,” and that calling it “ancillary” risks recreating look-through by another name. But that objection assumes the §§ 9–11 request is a new, freestanding proceeding; where, as the Chief stresses, the district court entered a § 3 stay (not a dismissal), the same Article III “case” remains pending, and nothing in the FAA’s text says jurisdiction self-destructs during the pause. Smith v. Spizzirri, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, reinforces that § 3 is designed precisely to hold the federal action in place so the parties may return to it—making the post-award motion a continuation step, not a jurisdictional end-run. Badgerow still governs standalone, newly filed post-award applications; it does not compel us to invent a midstream jurisdictional “reset” that the statute does not prescribe.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Badgerow requires an independent jurisdictional basis for a §§ 9–11 “application,” and that ancillary/supplemental labels risk recreating look-through jurisdiction. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that this misreads Badgerow as imposing a midstream “jurisdictional reset” even when the court already had undisputed original jurisdiction and merely entered the mandatory § 3 stay; a stay preserves the same civil action rather than terminating it as in Kokkonen. Smith v. Spizzirri reinforces that § 3 is designed so the parties can return to the same federal case after arbitration, which makes it hard to say Congress silently stripped the court of power to finish that case with the ordinary post-award steps. Limiting the holding to post-award motions filed in the same, still-pending stayed action avoids any broad circumvention of Badgerow while serving administrability and institutional legitimacy concerns.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s ancillary-jurisdiction framing—that a § 3 stay keeps the “action” pending so confirmation/vacatur is just the next step—has force, but it cannot be reconciled with Badgerow’s textual line between § 4 (look-through permitted) and §§ 9–11 (look-through barred) without functionally restoring look-through through the back door. Even if § 3 contemplates a single stayed “action,” the FAA still labels the post-award request an “application” under §§ 9–11, and Badgerow insists jurisdiction must appear on the face of that application; docket continuity cannot supply statutory subject-matter jurisdiction Congress withheld. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s appeal to ordinary ancillary/supplemental principles (including § 1367) is likewise in tension with Badgerow’s premise that courts may not use background jurisdictional doctrines to overcome the FAA’s deliberate jurisdictional structure for post-award proceedings. Smith v. Spizzirri, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, supports the procedural point that stays keep the case on the docket, but it did not purport to create or preserve Title 28 jurisdiction for a distinct post-award adjudication that, in substance, presents only state-law vacatur/confirmation grounds.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Alito raise the hardest point: Badgerow’s insistence that a §§ 9–11 “application” show an independent jurisdictional basis, and the worry that treating post-award motions as “ancillary” recreates look-through jurisdiction by another name. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, a § 3 stay does not terminate a properly invoked federal civil action; it preserves the court’s authority to bring that same action to completion, and unlike Kokkonen there is no dismissal-triggered jurisdictional reset that would require a new grant. Read pragmatically and in light of Smith v. Spizzirri (as Justice Kavanaugh notes), requiring a second, freestanding jurisdictional showing midstream would force duplicative filings and forum fragmentation with little textual support in § 3’s stay mechanism, while Badgerow can be cabined to standalone, newly initiated post-award proceedings. On my procedural-fairness and administrability lens, continuing jurisdiction in the stayed action is the narrower rule that respects Badgerow’s line without turning § 3 into a trapdoor.

John Roberts.reasoning: Where the district court properly had original jurisdiction over the underlying action and entered a FAA § 3 stay, the case remains pending on the court’s docket, and the court may resolve the parties’ post-arbitration requests to confirm or vacate as proceedings ancillary to that same action, without demanding a new, independent jurisdictional hook. Unlike Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994), which rejected enforcement jurisdiction after dismissal absent retained jurisdiction or incorporation, a § 3 stay does not terminate the case; it preserves the court’s control over the action while arbitration proceeds. The FAA’s rule that it does not itself supply jurisdiction (as reiterated in Badgerow) does not compel treating a stayed, already-jurisdictionally-proper case as if it were a brand-new, freestanding application under §§ 9–10, and requiring such a “second jurisdictional showing” would create unnecessary procedural complexity with little institutional upside. A narrow holding limited to stayed cases with undisputed original jurisdiction best aligns with precedent, federalism, and the Court’s interest in administrable rules.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s text contemplates a single, continuous federal “action” that may be stayed for arbitration under § 3, not dismissed and refiled, and nothing in §§ 9–10 requires a new, freestanding jurisdictional grant when the court is already properly exercising Article III jurisdiction over the pending case. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), holds only that a stand-alone §§ 9–11 application must itself show an independent jurisdictional basis; it does not strip a federal court of jurisdiction it already had over a still-pending, stayed action. Ordinary jurisdictional principles allow a federal court to resolve post-arbitration confirmation/vacatur motions as part of the same case, and to the extent a “hook” is needed, those motions fall within the court’s supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(a) because they are part of the same case or controversy as the stayed claims. Requiring a new jurisdictional basis after a § 3 stay would effectively manufacture a jurisdictional loss not found in the Constitution or the relevant statutes, contrary to the textually grounded approach Badgerow demanded.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FAA “bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction” on its own, and Badgerow v. Walters holds that applications under FAA §§ 9–11 require an independent jurisdictional basis apparent on the face of the application rather than derivable from the underlying dispute. 596 U.S. 1, 8–9 (2022). A § 3 stay keeps the original federal case administratively pending, but it does not expand Article III or Congress’s jurisdictional grants to cover a distinct post-award request that, under the FAA’s text and structure, is a separate “application” for confirmation or vacatur. Treating the stayed case as an automatic jurisdictional conduit would risk an end-run around Badgerow’s rule and the settled principle that subject-matter jurisdiction must exist for the specific relief sought, with predictable practical consequences of drawing purely state-law confirmation/vacatur disputes into federal court without a statutory hook.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When a district court properly has original jurisdiction over a civil action and enters the mandatory stay required by FAA § 3, that action remains pending on the court’s docket, so the court retains jurisdiction to resolve post-arbitration motions filed in the same case without demanding a new, freestanding jurisdictional hook. Badgerow v. Walters limits “look-through” jurisdiction for standalone FAA §§ 9–10 applications, but it does not require jurisdiction to evaporate in an already-filed federal-question (or diversity) action that was merely stayed rather than dismissed. Reading the FAA to force parties—often employees or consumers with limited resources—to start a new federal case (or be shunted into parallel state proceedings) to confirm or vacate an award would undermine fair, efficient access to justice and invite wasteful forum fragmentation. Vaden v. Discover Bank confirms the FAA is procedural and operates against an existing jurisdictional backdrop; here, Title 28 jurisdiction was present at the outset and continues through the stayed proceeding.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Once a federal court properly has original jurisdiction and issues a mandatory stay under FAA § 3, the action remains pending in federal court; post-arbitration motions to confirm/vacate/modify under FAA §§ 9–10 are best understood as ancillary to resolving that same live case and effectuating the stay’s purpose in a workable, coherent way. Badgerow v. Walters, 596 U.S. 1 (2022), which bars “look-through” jurisdiction for standalone §§ 9–10 applications, does not require a court to reestablish a new jurisdictional basis when the court is already exercising jurisdiction over a still-open case and is asked to complete the arbitral phase it supervised. Vaden v. Discover Bank, 556 U.S. 49 (2009), and Smith v. Spizzirri, 601 U.S. 472 (2024), reinforce that the FAA’s stay/compel mechanisms operate within cases that belong in federal court in the first place; reading §§ 9–10 to require a fresh jurisdictional hook midstream would create needless procedural fragmentation and undercut statutory workability. Consistent with ancillary-jurisdiction principles (see Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)), the court may decide the post-arbitration motions in the stayed action without demanding an independent jurisdictional basis anew.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Nothing in FAA § 3 suggests that a mandatory stay divests a federal court of the subject-matter jurisdiction it properly possessed when the action commenced; a stay pauses proceedings but does not terminate the case. When the same civil action remains pending, post-arbitration requests to confirm/vacate/modify under FAA §§ 9–11 are best understood as further proceedings in that case, not a new suit requiring a fresh jurisdictional “hook,” and any residual concern is addressed by supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367. Badgerow’s insistence on an independent jurisdictional basis for a stand-alone § 9/§ 10 application does not control where the federal court already has original jurisdiction over the underlying action and has merely stayed it. Consistent with separation-of-powers and textual limits, we should not invent a jurisdiction-stripping rule absent statutory direction, and Smith v. Spizzirri confirms the court’s ongoing supervisory role after a § 3 stay.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: When a district court has proper original jurisdiction and, on a party’s request, stays the action under FAA §3 “until … arbitration has been had,” the case remains pending in federal court, and the court retains continuing jurisdiction to take the next procedural step in that same action—adjudicating the parties’ post-arbitration motions under FAA §§9–10—without requiring a new, independent jurisdictional hook. Smith v. Spizzirri (2024) confirms that §3’s mandatory stay is designed so “the parties can return to federal court” after arbitration, which reflects the traditional, workable understanding that a stay preserves (rather than terminates) the court’s jurisdiction over the case. Requiring a fresh jurisdictional showing for post-arbitration motions inside the same stayed case would be impractical and would undermine §3’s structure by forcing bifurcation and forum shopping, while not being compelled by the FAA’s text. Badgerow’s limits on jurisdiction for standalone §§9–10 applications do not control where the confirmation/vacatur request is made in the same action that already properly invoked federal jurisdiction and was merely stayed, not dismissed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The FAA “bestow[s] no federal jurisdiction but rather require[s] an independent jurisdictional basis” for applications under §§ 9–11, and Badgerow v. Walters holds that such jurisdiction must appear on the face of the confirmation/vacatur application itself rather than by looking through to the underlying dispute. Nothing in § 3’s stay mechanism supplies continuing federal subject-matter jurisdiction for post-award relief, and treating a stayed case as an automatic jurisdictional conduit would effectively circumvent Badgerow’s textual line between § 4 (look-through permitted) and §§ 9–11 (look-through barred). Although the stayed action remains pending procedurally, Article III and Congress’s jurisdictional statutes still require a statutory grant for the post-award application; absent diversity or a federal question on the application’s face, federal courts must decline. Precedent respecting the FAA’s structure and Badgerow’s methodologically consistent textual reading therefore supports requiring an independent jurisdictional basis for the post-arbitration motions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Where a federal court properly had original jurisdiction over the civil action and entered a mandatory stay under FAA § 3, that case remains pending on the court’s docket, and the court’s continuing adjudicatory authority over the action should include resolving the case-dispositive post-arbitration motions that the stay contemplated (confirmation/vacatur/modification). Badgerow v. Walters held that FAA §§ 9–10 do not themselves supply jurisdiction and rejected “look-through” for standalone confirmation/vacatur applications, but it did not address—much less foreclose—the court’s retention of jurisdiction in an already-valid federal case merely stayed for arbitration rather than dismissed. Treating the post-arbitration motions as part of the same stayed action best fits § 3’s structure and promotes procedural fairness and practical consequences by avoiding pointless duplicative filings and jurisdictional gamesmanship after the federal court has already properly assumed the case. Vaden v. Discover Bank’s recognition that FAA jurisdictional analysis depends on the specific FAA mechanism reinforces that §§ 9–10 limits do not require a second, independent jurisdictional “reset” when the court is simply completing the stayed federal action.
